- **New-MtTest:** [Writes the new test files with `-Encoding utf8`](https://github.com/maester365/maester/blob/506064a0147a54085f01d00797c169820a709a60/powershell/public/run/New-MtTest.ps1#L215-L218), which produces UTF-8 without BOM in PowerShell 7.

| Area | with BOM | without | of those, containing non-ASCII |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

So **66.1% carry a BOM**. The convention holds almost perfectly where the shipped tests live (261 of 267) and mostly does not hold anywhere else.

## Why CI is green anyway

`PSUseBOMForUnicodeEncodedFile` is **not** excluded — `powershell/tests/general/PSScriptAnalyzer.Tests.ps1` excludes only `PSAvoidTrailingWhitespace` and `PSShouldProcess`, and `powershell/tests/pester.ps1:264` even prints a fix script when that rule fires. The rule works: I ran it directly on the eight BOM-less files that contain non-ASCII and **all eight raise it** as a Warning (positive control: a file with a BOM, `powershell/public/run/Invoke-Maester.ps1`, raises nothing).

The reason none of them ever fails a build is the analyzed path set. `PSScriptAnalyzer.Tests.ps1:6` is:

```powershell
$CommandPath = @("$PSScriptRoot/../../public/", "$PSScriptRoot/../../internal/")
```

That is **457 files, 27.3% of the tree**. The other 1,214 are never analyzed — and all eight violations are outside it:

| File | Area |
| --- | --- |
| `tests/maester/entra/Test.MT.1024.ps1` | shipped test |
| `tests/maester/defender/Test.MT.1059.ps1` | shipped test |
| `powershell/tests/functions/Get-MtAffectedObject.Tests.ps1` | unit test |
| `powershell/tests/functions/Get-MtHtmlReport.Tests.ps1` | unit test |

| `powershell/tests/functions/Test-MtContext.Tests.ps1` | unit test |
| `powershell/tests/functions/ZeroTrustAssessmentPack.Tests.ps1` | unit test |
| `build/Update-MaesterConfigVersion.ps1` | build script |

Two of those are the family tests `MT.1024` and `MT.1059`, which ship to users.

## The part that decides what the convention can be

You already noticed it for the ASCII case, and it generalises: **`PSUseBOMForUnicodeEncodedFile` only fires on files that contain non-ASCII.** Of the 566 BOM-less files, it can ever see 8. So the rule is not a mechanism for "all `.ps1` files carry a BOM" — it is a mechanism for "a file that *needs* a BOM has one", which is the narrower claim that matters for Windows PowerShell 5.1 reading accented characters.

That means the documented convention and the available enforcement are two different rules, which is, I think, the real source of the confusion you hit.

## Two ways out, and they are different decisions

1. **Keep the convention as written** (every `.ps1` and `.psm1` is UTF-8 with BOM). Then PSScriptAnalyzer cannot enforce it and a separate check is needed: a three-byte prefix test over the tree, which is a handful of lines in a Pester test. It would currently fail on 566 files, so it needs a one-off sweep first — and the three generators (`New-MtTest`, the EIDSCA and ORCA updaters) have to change, or they reintroduce violations on every run.

Either way, **widening `$CommandPath` is the change with the most value for the least risk**, because today a rule that exists and works is pointed at a quarter of the repo.

Happy to send whichever you pick: the eight-file fix plus the path-set widening is small and safe; the repo-wide sweep plus a prefix test is bigger and touches 566 files, so I would not start it without @merill saying that is the convention he wants.

Measured on Linux, PowerShell 7 and PSScriptAnalyzer 1.25.0, reading the committed blobs rather than the working tree. What I did not check: whether any of the 566 would break under Windows PowerShell 5.1 in practice — for the 558 pure-ASCII ones there is nothing to break, and the 8 are the ones at risk.

content.text:
## Analysis: [maester365/maester#2663](https://github.com/maester365/maester/issues/2663): BOM convention for PowerShell files

**Status:** open, no labels and no assignee. Travis (thetechgy) asked whether every PowerShell file is meant to be UTF-8 with BOM, because `New-MtTest` and the EIDSCA and ORCA generators write files without one. SamErde said BOM is still the standard. earbona23 then measured the repo and offered to send a fix PR, but is waiting for you to pick the convention. SamErde's latest question is whether there's any downside to always using a BOM, and whether a failing CI check is worth the disruption.

### What I checked on current `main`
earbona's numbers are right. Two more files have been added since they counted:
- **Total:** 1,105 of 1,678 `.ps1`/`.psm1`/`.psd1` files have a BOM.
- **Consistent areas:** `tests/ad`, `tests/cis`, `tests/cisa` and `tests/asd` are all BOM.
- **Mixed areas:** `powershell/internal` (167 with, 212 without), `powershell/public` (49/30), `powershell/tests` (103/132) and `build/` (11/61).
- **Generated suites:** `tests/eidsca` and `tests/orca` have no BOM at all, and neither does `packs/`.
- **The 8 at-risk files** (BOM-less with non-ASCII) are the same 8 earbona listed. In `Test.MT.1024` and `Test.MT.1059` the non-ASCII characters are emoji (✅ ❌ ➡️ 🗄️) in result Markdown.
- **The analyzer gate** covers only `public/` and `internal/` ([PSScriptAnalyzer.Tests.ps1:6](powershell/tests/general/PSScriptAnalyzer.Tests.ps1:6)). `PSUseBOMForUnicodeEncodedFile` only fires on non-ASCII files, so it can never enforce "every file has a BOM".
- **Writers that drop the BOM:** `New-MtTest` and `Convert-MtTest` (`-Encoding utf8`), the EIDSCA and ORCA generators, and several other `build/` scripts. Some of those write JSON or Markdown, where no BOM is correct.
- **No `.editorconfig`.** Only `.vscode/settings.json` sets `utf8bom`, which is why files written outside VS Code (including by agents) come out mixed.

### What the thread is missing
1. **The original reason for the BOM no longer applies at runtime.** The BOM matters because Windows PowerShell 5.1 reads a BOM-less file as ANSI and garbles non-ASCII text. Maester is now `CompatiblePSEditions = 'Core'` with `PowerShellVersion = '7.4'`. PowerShell 7 reads BOM-less files as UTF-8, so none of the 8 files is broken today. That's consistent with Travis seeing no runtime failure. This is about consistency, not a live bug.
2. **The source encoding of module files doesn't reach users.** `Build-MaesterModule.ps1` merges `public/` and `internal/` into `Maester.psm1` and writes it with a BOM (line 590, `Set-Utf8BomContent`). So the 242 BOM-less module files ship with a BOM anyway. Only `tests/` and `packs/` are copied byte for byte (lines 843 and 855), and those are what users open in their own editors.

### Answering SamErde: downsides of always using a BOM
For `.ps1`/`.psm1`/`.psd1` the downsides are small:
- **Shebang scripts:** a `#!/usr/bin/env pwsh` script run directly on Linux or macOS breaks if the BOM comes before `#!`. I didn't check whether any repo scripts use a shebang, so check before a sweep.
- **The sweep diff:** one-off noise across about 570 files, plus first-line conflicts for any open PR that touches line 1 of those files.
- **Ongoing CI friction:** new files from generators and agents will fail until the writers are fixed. That's why the writers have to change first.

The upsides are one simple rule, no encoding guesswork when someone opens a file in Windows PowerShell ISE or an older editor, and agreement with PSScriptAnalyzer and the existing VS Code setting.

### My recommendation
Keep "always BOM" for `.ps1`, `.psm1` and `.psd1`, and enforce it with a simple byte check rather than PSScriptAnalyzer. Switching the 1,105 BOM files to no BOM would cause more churn than it saves. In this order:
1. **Fix the writers:**
   - `New-MtTest` and `Convert-MtTest` should use `-Encoding utf8BOM`.
   - The EIDSCA and ORCA generators should use `UTF8Encoding::new($true)` for `.ps1` only. Generated `.md` and JSON stay BOM-less.
   - Fix any other `build/` script that emits `.ps1`.
2. **Add an `.editorconfig`** with `[*.{ps1,psm1,psd1}] charset = utf-8-bom`. It covers editors other than VS Code and many agents.
3. **Do a one-off sweep** that adds the 3-byte prefix. Regenerate EIDSCA and ORCA rather than editing them by hand, per the generated-content rule. Run `pester.ps1` afterwards.
4. **Add a byte-prefix Pester test** under `powershell/tests/general/` covering the whole tree, with the auto-fix one-liner in its failure message, the way `pester.ps1` already does for the analyzer rule. This answers SamErde's disruption worry: the failure is cheap to fix.
5. **Widen the PSScriptAnalyzer path set to `tests/`** (earbona's point). It's worth doing for the other rules too, but it may surface new warnings, so it should be its own PR.
6. **Update `contributing.md`:** add `.psd1`, and say the BOM is a consistency rule because Maester is Core-only.

earbona offered to do the work. A reply with this ruling would unblock them. Splitting it into two PRs would keep the risk down: writers, `.editorconfig` and docs first, then the sweep with the check.

input.content:
Thanks @thetechgy for raising this, and for checking it against `main` with a reproduction instead of just a hunch. And thanks @earbona23 for measuring the whole tree. The table and the finding that PSScriptAnalyzer only ever looked at a quarter of the repo turned a style question into something we could actually decide. @SamErde, thanks for keeping it moving.

**The ruling: every `.ps1`, `.psm1` and `.psd1` file is UTF-8 with a BOM, and Markdown and JSON have none.**

One point that shaped this: Maester 3 runs only on PowerShell 7.4+ (`CompatiblePSEditions = 'Core'`), and PowerShell 7 reads BOM-less files as UTF-8. So the classic Windows PowerShell 5.1 reason for the BOM no longer applies at runtime. That's why nobody hit a failure, and why the eight BOM-less files with emoji work today. Also, the build already writes the merged `Maester.psm1` with a BOM, so the module files never shipped without one. Only `tests/` and `packs/` are copied as-is.

So this is a consistency rule, not a bug fix. We kept the BOM rather than dropping it because two-thirds of the tree, the VS Code settings, the contributing guide and PSScriptAnalyzer's rule all already assume it. Switching the other way would mean more churn, and the BOM still helps anyone opening a test in Windows PowerShell ISE or an older editor.

On @SamErde's question about downsides: for these file types there aren't many. The one real one is that a BOM before a `#!/usr/bin/env pwsh` shebang breaks direct execution on Linux and macOS, and no tracked PowerShell file has a shebang. The cost of the CI check is kept low because the failure message prints the one-line fix.

As @earbona23 pointed out, PSScriptAnalyzer can't enforce "every file", so #<PR> enforces it with a byte check instead:

- `New-MtTest`, `Convert-MtTest`, `New-MtPack`, and the EIDSCA and ORCA generators now write PowerShell files with a BOM (Markdown without), so they stop reintroducing the problem.
- A new `.editorconfig` sets `utf-8-bom` for PowerShell files, for editors and agents that don't use our VS Code settings.
- A one-off sweep adds the BOM to the 573 files that were missing it. It only adds the three bytes, with no other content changes.
- `powershell/tests/general/FileEncoding.Tests.ps1` checks every tracked PowerShell file, and checks the scaffolding commands and generators.
- `contributing.md` now covers `.psd1`, explains why, and fixes the suggested one-liner, which used `Out-File` and added an extra trailing newline.

@earbona23, thanks for offering to send this. It touched a lot of files at once, so I put it together in one go to keep conflicts with open PRs short. Your other suggestion, widening the PSScriptAnalyzer path set to cover `tests/` and `powershell/tests/`, is still open and would be very welcome as a follow-up PR. It will probably surface some new warnings from other rules, so it's better as its own change.

If you have an open PR, merging `main` after #<PR> lands should be clean unless you edited the first line of an existing file. New `.ps1` files need the BOM, and the test will tell you if one is missing.
